reason: 40:3–4 complete the beatitude: the Lord’s promised protection of the one who considers the poor, which the record’s own note cites.
Praise of the royal bridegroom: the reported anointing gives no charge or direction (doctrine/praise); Hebrews 1:9’s quotation is likewise unrecorded.

context: A petition’s reason clause echoes 145:3: human salvation is vain (repeated at Greek Psalm 107:13).
reason: Prayer to God, so no record of its own, but its ground restates the recorded maxim against trusting mortals; link only.

context: The psalm’s closing wish repeats the call for all the earth’s ends to fear God.
reason: 66:4–6 are jussives addressed to God in prayer (out of scope); 66:8 repeats the recorded call of 32:8, so link it.
Address to God recounting the wicked’s downfall: narrative and doctrine within prayer; AUD-21-72-16 rightly keeps only the lesson of 72:27–28.
The same coalition rulers’ plot quoted again (‘Let us inherit God’s sanctuary’), as the record’s note says; same speakers and occasion.
Quoted ‘Return, sons of men’ inside a prayer is most likely the decree of mortality (89:4–6), not a call to repent; cannot be verified.
David’s own resolve and past conduct addressed to God (‘I will make music… I used to walk’): a speaker’s plan, not a direction.
Narrator’s purpose clause closing the history psalm: doctrine about why the land was given; it recalls no specific recorded direction.
Agur’s petition is a prayer addressed to God, out of scope; the catalogue likewise leaves Sirach 23:1–6 and Wisdom 9 unrecorded.
The cycles of generations, sun, wind and streams are the premise of ‘all things are wearisome… nothing new’ (1:8–11); same speaker and poem.

context: Qoheleth first observes that God gave humans a grievous distraction, the saying repeated at 3:10.
reason: 1:13 is not the twisted/lacking maxim of AUD-23-1-12; its saying repeats 3:10, inside AUD-23-3-9.
The brothers’ conditional, figurative plan for their sister (‘let us build battlements’) is their own deliberation, not a direction; Song dialogue is mostly Study Context.
Zion renews the same appeal (‘Hear… all you peoples, and see my pain’) in the same lament; attach to that Study Context record.
Prediction that the righteous will judge nations directs no one; the editor limited AUD-26-3-5 to the teaching of 3:9.
Narrative introduction to the ungodly’s speech (5:4–13) in a judgment forecast; no direction, and the speech’s lesson is recorded at AUD-26-5-6.
The writer announces what he himself will declare: a speaker’s own plan, not a direction; AUD-26-6-22 rightly begins at 6:23.
Narrator’s account of how image worship spread ‘at rulers’ commands’: a custom described, with no specific ruler, order or speaker.
Reported attitude of the idol-maker, condemned by the narrator; the counter-teaching (do not seek gain from evil) is implied, not stated.

context: The serpent episode states the same lesson: not herb or poultice but God’s word healed them.
reason: Same writer’s lesson as 16:26 (God’s word, not natural means, preserves), applied to the healing; restatement, so link.
Historical judgment in the retelling (Egypt worse than Sodom); the hospitality lesson is implied, not stated as a direction.
Body of the message Isaiah must deliver (7:4–9; 7:9 already linked): the plot is quoted only to be annulled. Not a separate plan record.
Prophetic portrait of the coming king’s judging: prediction, not a direction, and not a quotation of K015’s ‘judge with righteous judgment’.
Future scripted taunt (‘you will take up this lament… on that day’): prediction of Israel’s song, not a present direction; cf. Study Context 12:4.

title: Moab’s devourers are told to trample its vineyards as far as Iazer
speaker: the Lord through Isaiah (oracle against Moab)
recipient: the devourers of nations (invaders of Moab)
topic: Historical commissions, journeys and public life
reason: Explicit summons to attackers, like recorded Jeremiah 5:10; low because the surrounding Greek-based lines are obscure.

title: The watchman tells the inquirer from Seir to seek and stay near
speaker: the watchman in Isaiah’s vision
topic: Historical commissions, journeys and public life
reason: The watchman’s reply to the recorded call of 21:11 adds his own direction (‘seek, and dwell beside me’); different speaker, so not an extension.

title: The ships of Carthage are told to wail over Tyre’s fall
speaker: the Lord through Isaiah (oracle concerning Tyre)
topic: Historical commissions, journeys and public life
reason: Wail summons opening and closing the Tyre oracle, like published AUD-28-13-6; same as R3a draft GAP-28-23-1, record once.

title: The earth’s people are told to wail over the vanished wine
speaker: the Lord through Isaiah
topic: Historical commissions, journeys and public life
reason: Explicit wail summons in the world-judgment oracle, of the kind published at Isaiah 13:6 and 15:2; addressee is the earth’s inhabitants (24:6).

title: Hope belongs to the devout; woe to those who reject the law
speaker: voices from the ends of the earth (Isaiah’s oracle)
reason: Woe-saying naming a sin, like the published Isaiah woes (AUD-28-5-8); low because it is reported, future speech in the oracle.
Greek-based imperative with no identifiable addressee and unclear object (‘hand all these things over’): cannot be verified with sufficient context.
Summons ‘Women coming from a spectacle, come!’ states no purpose or task; obscure Greek-based line, so it cannot be verified with sufficient context.
36:5–10 completes the message Rapsakes tells the officials to deliver (36:4), including the horse wager (36:8) and claimed divine sanction (36:10).
The answer to Israel’s complaint in the same address: the unwearied God strengthens those who endure for Him. Completes the record’s passage.
‘Know… see’ closes the idol satire with the lesson that 44:21’s ‘Remember these things’ refers to; the same appeal to Israel.

context: Isaiah: had Israel listened to God’s commands, its peace would have been like a river.
reason: Not a direction itself, but the same recorded teaching as Greek Psalm 80:12–15 (what obedience would have brought); link, not a new record.
Lament that the righteous perish unheeded: observation and doctrine; ‘See’ is rhetorical and no direction or rule of life is stated.
Sarcastic jussive to idolaters (‘let them rescue you’) and a conditional promise to the faithful; neither directs anyone.

context: Earlier indictment: Israel, denying its pollution, is told to see its ways in the valley and know what it did.
reason: Same rhetorical call to look at the evidence of defilement as 3:2 (a Study Context record); link rather than a separate record.

title: The message is to be announced to Jacob and proclaimed in Judah
speaker: the Lord through Jeremiah
topic: Historical commissions, journeys and public life
reason: Explicit summons to proclaim, like published AUD-29-4-16 and AUD-29-31-4; it introduces the Study Context address of 5:21.
Rhetorical question and declaration that Judah’s offerings are unacceptable: indictment, not a direction; the catalogue keeps Amos 5:21–22 as Study Context.
7:22–23 is one sentence: God did not command sacrifice but ‘Hear My voice’. 7:22 is the contrast half of the recorded recollection.

context: Jeremiah confesses the same truth: a person’s way is not his own, nor can he direct his course.
reason: A prayer, so no record of its own, but it restates Proverbs 20:24’s maxim; link as Additional Scripture.

title: Egypt’s routed troops urge one another to flee home
speaker: Egypt’s soldiers (quoted in the oracle)
topic: Historical commissions, journeys and public life
reason: Quoted mutual exhortation (‘Let us rise and return’), the kind recorded at Jeremiah 28:9–10 and 6:4–5.
Isolated imperative inside first-person divine speech, with no stated addressee or purpose: cannot be verified with sufficient context.
Closing sentence of the same Rechabite reply: why, despite the tent rule, they now live in Jerusalem. Same speakers and occasion.

title: The officials agree to report all the scroll’s words to the king
speaker: the officials (rulers) of Judah
topic: Historical commissions, journeys and public life
reason: Mutual resolution (‘Let us… report’), like recorded 2 Kings 7:9; a different direction from the summons in AUD-29-43-14, so not an extension.
Isolated alarm cry with no stated addressee and an obscure clause (‘judge everything’); adjacent 7:12 jussives are only Study Context. Cannot be verified.

title: Jerusalem is told to bear her shame for outdoing her sisters
speaker: the Lord through Ezekiel
reason: Explicit imperatives to Jerusalem (‘receive your torment… be ashamed’), comparable to recorded Ezekiel 36:32; a distinct oracle, so a separate record.
Foretold burial procedure (‘they will designate men’): prediction of what Israel will do, not a direction to anyone.
2:2 is the reported summons to report the dream and 2:8–9 the renewed demand: same king, occasion and direction, as the record’s note says.

context: Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges that the three rejected his command and chose the furnace rather than serve another god.
reason: The doxology is praise (not the 3:96 decree), but it expressly recalls the king’s bow-or-burn command; link it there.

context: Daniel reports the same charge: in Cyrus’s first year the messenger told him to be strong and take courage.
reason: Narrator restates the messenger’s charge of 10:19 (‘take courage and be strong’); associated verse, link as Additional Scripture.
Narrative of the false witnesses performing the rite, without quoting or citing Leviticus 24:14; plain narrative is not linked.
Obscure figurative imperative with an unstated addressee (Greek-based text); cannot be verified with sufficient context, cf. Joel 4:13 kept as Study Context.

title: Israel’s love of its Bethel and Gilgal rites is to be announced
speaker: the Lord through Amos
reason: Explicit summons to proclaim Israel’s guilt, like recorded Amos 3:9 and 3:13; low because the addressee is unnamed and the tone indicting.
Rhetorical question in an encouragement oracle; the maxim ‘do not despise small beginnings’ is implied, not stated.
Rest of the message Zechariah is told to speak (6:12–15), ending with its condition: ‘if you truly listen to the voice of the Lord’.

title: The devil demands Jesus make bread, leap down and worship him
speaker: the devil (the tempter)
reason: Solicitations to sin are recorded (Potiphar’s wife AUD-01-39-7, Job 2:9). Origin is non-divine. Link Luke 4:3, 5–7, 9–11 as Additional Scripture.
Repeats coverage: included in the record proposed at V132 (Matthew 4:3, 5–6, 8–9), one record for all three demands.
The disciples’ plea for rescue is a petition, and Jesus’ reply is a rhetorical rebuke; the storm scene states no recordable direction.

title: Jesus tells the healed woman to take courage: her faith saved her
speaker: Jesus
recipient: the woman with the flow of blood
reason: AUD-46-8-43’s note calls Matthew’s ‘Take courage’ distinct from ‘go in peace’; record it as AUD-44-9-2 records the same words.

title: The returning unclean spirit warns of a worse end for this generation
speaker: Jesus
recipient: the scribes and Pharisees seeking a sign
reason: Distinct warning parable closing the sign discourse; the editor kept it out of AUD-44-12-22. Link Luke 11:24–26 as Additional Scripture.

context: Jesus affirms that the promised Elijah, who restores all things, has already come in John the Baptist.
reason: Expressly recalls Malachi’s Elijah promise; better target than AUD-46-7-24, which concerns the messenger saying. Mark 9:11–13 likewise.

context: In the temple the chief priests object to the children’s hosannas; Jesus defends the praise with Psalm 8:3.
reason: The objection is implied, so no record of its own, but it parallels the recorded demand to silence praise of Jesus.

context: Matthew records Jesus’ defence of the woman who anointed Him for burial, as Mark 14:6–9 does.
reason: Synoptic form of the Bethany defence; link Jesus’ words as the Mark 14:6–9 entry does (R6a’s draft proposes 26:6–13).

context: At the arrest Jesus again tells Judas to go ahead: ‘Friend, do what you have come for.’
reason: Separate from Judas’s signal (per AUD-44-26-47’s note); it repeats Jesus’ word to Judas in John 13:27 on a new occasion.
Mocking taunt (‘Prophesy to us… who struck Thee?’), not a direction meant to be obeyed; the catalogue does not record such taunts.
Taunts at the cross (‘save Thyself… come down’) are mockery, not directions; the parallel taunt of Greek Psalm 21:9 is also unrecorded.
Bystanders’ mocking aside (‘let us see whether Elijah comes’) is a taunt, not a direction or resolution with any purpose.

context: Mark’s summary: Jesus heals many and sternly warns the unclean spirits not to make Him known.
reason: Mark’s form of Matthew 12:15–16’s charge; 3:9 is its own record (AUD-45-3-9), so excluded. Same as R6a draft.
‘Be silent; be still’ addresses wind and sea (nature speech, cf. unrecorded Joshua 10:12); 4:40 is a rhetorical rebuke whose direction is implied.

title: Jesus sends the Syrophoenician woman home: the demon has left her daughter
speaker: Jesus
reason: Healing dismissal like John 4:50 (AUD-47-4-46). Same event as R3b draft GAP-44-15-21: keep one record, other gospel as Additional Scripture.

context: Mark’s form of the rebuke in Matthew 16:8–11 (inside K086), completing the linked Mark 8:14–16.
reason: K086’s own passage includes this rebuke (Matthew 16:8–11); the Mark link stops at 8:16, leaving its parallel 8:17–21 unattached.
Peter’s offer to build tents (‘he did not know what to answer’) is a speaker’s own proposal, not a direction; Luke 9:33 likewise.
